The new page had more signups because it received twice as many visitors, but a smaller share signed up: 160 of 2,000 visitors (8%), compared with 100 of 1,000 (10%) on the old page. The observed conversion rate was lower on the new page. These are descriptive results; without a significance analysis, we can't establish whether the difference reflects more than chance.

A database index works like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up and go straight to the relevant pages. Similarly, a database can use an index to locate matching rows without checking every row in a table.

For example, if an app often searches for a customer by email address, an index on the email column can make those searches faster.

The tradeoff is storage and extra work when data changes. When you insert, update, or delete relevant data, the database must also maintain the index, which can slow writes. Not every query benefits from an index, so choose indexes based on the searches your app actually performs.

Daily totals count each person once per day; the weekly total counts each person once for the whole week. Someone visiting Monday and Tuesday adds one to each day's count but only one to the week's count. That's why adding the daily numbers can give a different total; it's expected, not a reporting error. We should label the views “daily unique visitors” and “weekly unique visitors” to make this clearer.

We don't yet know whether the emails reduced missed appointments. The rate fell from 18% in August to 12% in September, when reminders began, but September also had a different mix of appointment types and a new cancellation policy. With no randomized comparison, this shows an association, not a demonstrated causal effect. Next, compare like-for-like appointment types and, if feasible, test reminders using randomized assignment.
